summary: This informational memo from Cabletron specifies the protocol between a switch's connection control entity and an external flow admission server. It is a vendor protocol rather than a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The doorman at a club asks the manager inside whether each guest may come in.

questions: how does a switch request flow admission
what is a flow admission service
subtitle: A protocol for switches to ask permission before admitting network flows.

tldr.problem: Network switches need to enforce policies on which flows they accept, but the policy logic is complex and vendor-specific. Each switch cannot implement all possible policies.
tldr.mechanism: LFAP lets a switch's control entity query an external Flow Admission Service (FAS) before accepting a flow. The FAS responds with admission decisions and operating policies that the switch enforces.
tldr.outcome: Policies can be centralized in a dedicated service, freeing switches from policy complexity. This vendor protocol was informational; it competed with standardized approaches.

facts.label: Number of message types
facts.value: 9 (FAR, FAA, FAU, FUN, FUA, FCR, FCA, AR, ARA)

today: RFC 2124 is an Informational RFC published by Cabletron Systems and has not been obsoleted. It documents a vendor-specific protocol rather than a standard. Centralized flow admission control via separate services has evolved into modern network policy engines and SDN controllers.

sections.title: What LFAP Does
sections.content:
Light-weight Flow Admission Protocol (LFAP) defines how a network switch's call control entity (CCE) communicates with an external Flow Admission Service (FAS). Before setting up a flow, the switch sends a Flow Admission Request (FAR) to the FAS, describing the flow with details like source and destination addresses, service type, and client data. The FAS decides whether to allow it, deny it, or apply operating policies (such as priority or bandwidth limits) and sends back a Flow Admission Acknowledge (FAA) message.

Once a flow is running, the switch periodically updates the FAS on the flow's status via Flow Update Notification (FUN) messages, which report byte counts and packet counts. The FAS can also send Flow Change Requests (FCR) to adjust policy or stop a flow. This design lets network managers centralize policy logic without modifying the switch firmware.
sections.plainLanguage: The switch asks permission before starting a flow. If yes, the switch keeps telling the manager how much data is going through, and the manager can tell the switch to stop or change the speed.

sections.title: Message Structure
sections.content:
All LFAP messages share a common 8-octet header: Version, Op Code (operation type), Reserved bits, Status, Message ID, and Message Length. Following the header are Information Elements (IEs), each with a 2-octet TYPE, 2-octet LENGTH, and variable-length VALUE. All IEs are padded to 4-octet alignment.

The nine operation codes are: FAR (1), FAA (2), FAU (3, update), FUN (4), FUA (5), FCR (6), FCA (7), AR (8, administrative request), and ARA (9, acknowledge). Status values are SUCCESS (0), CORRUPTED (1), and VERSION (2). Message IDs associate requests with responses and must be unique while a message is pending.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message has a label saying what kind of message it is, who sent it, and what information is attached. It's like a form with blanks you fill in.

sections.title: Information Elements
sections.content:
IEs encode the flow details and policies. Common IEs include Flow ID (a prefix from the FAS plus a local ID to uniquely identify a flow), Source Address and Destination Address (the flow endpoints), Flow State (ACTIVE or INACTIVE), and counting IEs: Byte Count (Type 1 for cumulative, Type 2 for delta since last update) and Packet Count (Types 3 and 4, similar). Policy IEs come in two flavors: optional (Type 9, safe to ignore) and mandatory (Type 10, or the switch must abort). Policy IDs beginning with 01xx control usage constraints; 02xx handle routing policies; 03xx cover administrative settings like Keep Statistics, Connection Priority, Checkpoint Timer (how often to send FUN), and Checkpoint Threshold (byte count to trigger FUN).

Proprietary policies use Object Identifier (OID) format (Types 11 and 12) so vendors can experiment without breaking the protocol. A Multiple Record IE (Type 18) bundles multiple flows into one update to reduce overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of IEs as tags that carry information: who this flow is from and to, how many bytes have gone through, and what rules apply to it.

sections.title: The Request-Response Cycle
sections.content:
The switch initiates by sending a FAR with Source Address, Destination Address, Flow ID, Time, and optional Service Identifier and Client Data. The FAS responds with a FAA containing a Status field and may include optional or mandatory policies, an alternate destination (for redirection), or a Flow Failure Code (0 = policy reject, 1 = unknown flow, 2 = duplicate request, 3 = unknown destination). If the switch does not understand a mandatory policy, it sends back a FAU (update) message with an error code and the FAS returns a FUA.

During the flow lifetime, the switch sends FUN messages with updated counts and flow state. The FAS replies with FUA acknowledgements. The FAS can proactively send a FCR to change policy or stop the flow; the switch responds with FCA. Either party can initiate an Administrative Request (AR) for administrative operations such as requesting a new flow prefix; the other party answers with ARA.
sections.plainLanguage: The switch asks, the FAS answers. Then they keep talking while the flow runs, with the FAS able to say 'stop the flow' and the switch saying 'here's the count now'.

sections.title: Reliability and Error Handling
sections.content:
If a message arrives with an unknown version, the receiver responds with a generic FAILURE message (Status = VERSION, no IEs). A corrupted message (Status = CORRUPTED) gets the same treatment. The protocol relies on TCP for reliable delivery between the switch CCE and the FAS; the CCE must have IP reachability to the FAS and a preconfigured FAS IP address. A single registered port number (later IANA-assigned) is used for the TCP connection.

Error codes in FAA and FAU messages signal specific failures: a mandatory policy the switch does not understand triggers a policy error. The protocol does not define timeouts explicitly, but the reference to persistent message sending implies that switches should use retransmission if acknowledgements are delayed or lost.
sections.plainLanguage: If something goes wrong or doesn't make sense, the receiver says 'I don't understand that' instead of crashing. The switch and FAS talk over a reliable connection so messages do not get lost.
